strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: safety and concept removal in text-to-video diffusion models, an underexplored area relative to image diffusion unlearning.
Proposes a training-free, data-efficient approach requiring only 5 unsafe-safe prompt pairs and no retraining or original training data access.
The closed-form weight update embeds the refusal direction into model parameters without adding inference-time overhead, which is practically attractive.
Combines refusal vectors, low-rank subspace projection, and contrastive PCA in a plausible pipeline, with ablations on rank and suppression strength λ.
Includes qualitative results across multiple unsafe categories (pornography, gore, copyright/trademarks, public figures, sequential-action risk) and uses T2VSafetyBench, FVD, and MM-Notox metrics.
Discusses ethical risks and adversarial reversibility in the limitations section, showing some awareness of misuse concerns.
weaknesses: Significant novelty concern: the method largely combines existing ideas (refusal vectors, UCE/RECE-style weight editing, contrastive PCA) and adapts them to video; the core technical contribution over prior image unlearning work is incremental.
No comparison to any baseline unlearning methods (e.g., adapted UCE, RECE, fine-tuning, or inference-time safety filters), despite claiming advantages over surface-level filters.

The central claim that multimodal text+image conditioning improves concept extraction and prevents forgetting is not supported by any ablation or quantitative experiment; the appendix prompt lists are text-only, and it is unclear how image prompts are paired or used.

Mathematical inconsistency in the covariance computation: R is defined as H×N, but C_r =  ar R^T  ar R is claimed to be H×H; dimensionally this should be N×N unless R is N×H. The same issue appears for the retain-set covariance.

The closed-form weight update assumes a simple linear block x^{l+1}=W^{l+1}x^l, but the method is applied to FFN/cross-attention blocks containing LayerNorm, residual connections, and nonlinearities; the derivation does not justify that the correction can be exactly absorbed into those weights.

Evaluation is insufficient for a top-tier venue: only the original Open-Sora checkpoint is used as the baseline, with no statistical significance tests, no confidence intervals, and no human evaluation.

FVD is computed between original unsafe videos and censored videos rather than between generated videos and real data, so it does not measure standard generation fidelity or quality; the claim of preserved video quality is weakly supported.

MM-Notox improvements are very small (about 2–5%) and lack variance estimates; residual unsafe content remains high after unlearning (e.g., 33.0% copyright/trademarks, 13.4% pornography, 9.1% sequential-action risk).
The paper claims increased robustness against adversarial bypass attempts compared to input-output filters, but no adversarial evaluation or robustness experiment is provided.

Implementation details are under-specified: the choice of α in contrastive PCA, retain-set size and construction, exact layer activation extraction procedure, timestep selection for diffusion latents, and image-conditioning setup are not fully described.
Qualitative results appear cherry-picked; there is no systematic analysis of failure modes, flicker, temporal consistency, or collateral forgetting beyond limited examples.

Reproducibility remains questionable: although code is mentioned in the supplement, the main manuscript lacks enough detail for independent reimplementation, and the image-prompt pairs used for the claimed multimodal method are not shown.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely safety problem: removing harmful concepts from text-to-video diffusion models.
The proposed method is training-free and computationally efficient, requiring no retraining and no additional inference-time parameters or latency.
Uses few prompt pairs and does not require access to the original web-scale training data.
The combination of refusal-vector editing with low-rank/contrastive PCA is an interesting direction in principle, aiming to reduce collateral forgetting.
Provides qualitative examples across several unsafe categories and includes some implementation details/prompts.
The paper is generally well organized and includes a limitations/ethics warning.
weaknesses: Fundamental mathematical inconsistency: with N=5 prompt pairs, the covariance matrix dimensions and rank are inconsistent. If R is H×N, then R^T R is N×N, not H×H; if corrected to R R^T, its rank is at most N−1=4, so selecting k=100 principal components is impossible. This undermines the central low-rank cPCA claim.

The closed-form weight update assumes a single linear layer, but it is applied to FFN weights that contain nonlinear activations, LayerNorm, and residual connections. The derivation is not valid for the actual Transformer blocks without further justification.
No baselines: the paper compares only to the original Open-Sora model, with no comparison to UCE, RECE, fine-tuning, steering, or other unlearning methods adapted to video diffusion models.

The key claimed contribution of using multimodal (text+image) conditioning is not ablated. The appendix lists only text prompts and no image pairs, so the multimodal claim is unsupported and unreproducible.

Evaluation is invalid or insufficient: FVD is computed between original unsafe and censored generated videos, not against real video distributions, which is not the standard FVD quality metric. MM-Notox improvements are tiny (≈2–5%) and not validated.

Safety efficacy is weak: residual unsafe generation remains high, e.g., 33% for copyright/trademarks and 13.4% for pornography after intervention. This is unacceptable for safety-critical claims and contradicts “neutralizes” language.
Public figures baseline is only 10%, so the reduction to 2% is not compelling and may reflect selective category retention or low baseline difficulty.
GPT-4-based censorship evaluation lacks details: no exact evaluator prompt, no human validation, no confidence intervals or statistical tests, and no inter-rater reliability.
Claims of robustness against adversarial bypass attempts are untested. The method may only suppress explicit keywords and fail under paraphrases, synonyms, or jailbreak prompts.
The method is evaluated on only one video diffusion model (Open-Sora), so cross-model generalization is unknown.

Contrastive PCA uses SVD on a covariance difference C = C_r − α C_e, which is not guaranteed to be positive semidefinite; SVD is not the standard way to extract contrastive components, and no eigenvalue analysis is provided.

Reproducibility is limited: hyperparameters such as α, retain-set size, exact layer selection procedure, random seeds, generation parameters, and evaluator configuration are missing. Code is referenced but not included in the manuscript.

The “first training-free video unlearning” claim is not sufficient for novelty; the technical contribution is largely an adaptation of existing image/LLM erasure ideas with no rigorous new theory or strong empirical validation.

Ablations are incomplete: there is no quantitative comparison of text-only vs multimodal refusal vectors, no evaluation of collateral forgetting on unrelated capabilities, and no systematic study of multiple concepts.

Qualitative examples show incomplete removal in some cases (e.g., subjects remain partially undressed) and may simply replace concepts with semantically similar unsafe ones, rather than truly unlearning.
The paper does not discuss risks of permanently weighting the model, e.g., whether the edit can be inverted or whether repeated edits compound degradation.

strengths: Introduces the first training-free unlearning framework for video diffusion models, addressing a timely safety gap in text-to-video generation.
Requires only 5 safe/unsafe prompt pairs and uses a closed-form weight update, avoiding retraining, original training data, and inference overhead.
The low-rank refusal vector built from latent differences with contrastive PCA is a plausible and efficient mechanism for isolating target concepts and reducing collateral forgetting.
Provides both quantitative T2VSafetyBench results and qualitative examples across five unsafe categories, with large reductions in some categories (e.g., Gore from 74.9% to 5.3%).
Includes ablations on the cPCA rank k and suppression coefficient lambda, showing controllability and a censorship-vs-quality trade-off.
Discusses ethical limitations, including potential misuse and adversarial reversibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation lacks comparisons to any baseline method, such as simple refusal-vector subtraction, text-only extraction, adapted image unlearning methods like UCE/RECE, fine-tuning, or random-direction edits, so the advantage of the proposed low-rank cPCA design is not established.
Only one video diffusion backbone (Open-Sora) is tested; generalization to other video generators such as CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo, or ModelScopeT2V is unverified.

The FVD computation appears non-standard: it measures distance between original unsafe videos and censored videos rather than between real and generated video distributions, so it does not directly assess generation quality or prompt fidelity.
The key claim that multimodal text+image extraction preserves generation quality better than text-only is not supported by an ablation table or figure; the appendix only shows text prompt pairs.

The contrastive PCA uses SVD on C = C_r - alpha C_e, which is symmetric but indefinite. SVD orders by absolute singular values, not positive eigenvalues, so it may select directions more characteristic of the retain set rather than the forget set; eigendecomposition with positive-eigenvalue filtering would be more appropriate.
The contrastive PCA hyperparameter alpha is not reported and no sensitivity analysis is provided, limiting reproducibility and understanding of retention exclusion.
MM-Notox improvements are very small (1.85%-5.31%), and there is no statistical significance testing or human evaluation; GPT-4 frame-level judgments may be noisy.
The claim of robustness against adversarial bypass attempts is not evaluated with adversarial prompts or attacks.

The weight-editing derivation assumes a purely linear block x^{l+1}=W x^l, but typical transformer blocks contain LayerNorm and nonlinear operations between the edited activation and the updated weight matrix; the paper does not explain how exact absorption is achieved despite these operations.
The method removes only one concept at a time, and some unsafe categories retain substantial failure rates (e.g., Copyright and Trademarks still 33.0%), limiting practical utility.

strengths: Introduces the first training-free closed-form weight update framework for concept removal in video diffusion models, avoiding retraining and inference overhead.
Method is computationally efficient, requiring only five paired safe/unsafe prompts and a closed-form update, with a multi-concept extension.
Evaluates on two text-to-video models and two safety benchmarks, showing substantial censorship-rate reductions while often preserving FVD and prompt alignment.
Provides qualitative examples across multiple unsafe categories and includes ablations on rank, suppression strength, prompt-pair similarity, neutral-set choice, and cPCA vs. PCA.
Includes implementation details and code availability, supporting reproducibility to some extent.
weaknesses: The contrastive PCA step is technically problematic: it computes an SVD of the indefinite matrix C_r - alpha C_e. Since this matrix is symmetric but not necessarily positive semidefinite, singular values are absolute eigenvalues and may select directions with large negative contrast (neutral variance > unsafe variance), rather than the intended concept-specific directions. This requires eigendecomposition and positive-eigenvalue selection, or a clear justification for why SVD is valid here.

Evaluation is fragmented and lacks apples-to-apples comparisons: NullSCE is compared only on OPEN-SORA/T2VSafetyBench, SAFREE only on ZEROSCOPET2V/SafeSora, and FVD/MM-Notox are not reported for all baselines across all benchmarks. Important video unlearning baselines such as VideoEraser are not quantitatively compared.

Metric concerns: MM-Notox is defined as an embedding distance, which does not match the original metric name and shows only tiny or sometimes negative changes; GPT-4o judging alone is used without human validation; FVD reference data and computation protocol for text-to-video safety prompts are not clearly described.

Reproducibility is limited: the exact injection layer is ambiguously described as cross-attention modules, last FFN, and up-blocks across different models; the alpha value for the main cPCA experiments is not specified; activation pooling for video spatio-temporal features is not detailed; neutral prompts used for cPCA are not released.

Novelty is moderate: the method largely adapts existing ideas such as refusal vectors, UCE-style closed-form edits, and contrastive PCA to the video setting. The video-specific technical contributions are incremental, and the claimed joint use of text and image conditioning is not convincingly evaluated.

Ablations are incomplete: prompt-pair sensitivity, neutral-set resampling, and cPCA-vs-PCA comparisons are mostly limited to the Pornography subset, with no per-category statistical significance or full-benchmark validation.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: the paper claims preserved quality and semantic preservation, but MM-Notox worsens for some categories, FVD is not uniformly better, and the exact impact on safe-prompt generation quality is insufficiently quantified.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: safe generation and concept removal in video diffusion models.
Proposes a training-free, closed-form weight-update procedure with no inference-time overhead, which is practically appealing.
Combines refusal-vector ideas with contrastive low-rank subspace estimation to reduce collateral forgetting, a reasonable methodological direction.
Reports experiments on two video diffusion models and two safety benchmarks, with qualitative examples and ablations on rank, suppression strength, prompt pairs, and neutral prompts.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core mechanism is an adaptation of refusal-vector projection and closed-form weight editing already explored for LLMs and text-to-image diffusion, with low-rank cPCA added. The claimed 'first training-free weight update for video' is a narrow contribution and does not by itself establish top-tier significance.

The baseline comparisons are incomplete and not apples-to-apples. Table 1 compares only NullSCE on Open-Sora and reports only censorship for NullSCE, omitting FVD and MM-Notox. Table 2 compares only SAFREE on ZeroScopeT2V and omits FVD/MM-Notox for SAFREE. UCE is relegated to a single-category appendix study. Thus the central claim of outperforming state of the art is not supported across methods, models, and metrics.

The evaluation is confounded by model-benchmark pairing: Open-Sora is evaluated only on T2VSafetyBench and ZeroScopeT2V only on SafeSora. It is impossible to separate gains due to the method from model- or benchmark-specific effects. Cross-model and cross-benchmark evaluation is needed.

Censorship is judged by GPT-4o with no reported human validation, inter-rater agreement, or confidence intervals. Given the safety-critical nature of the task, the absence of variance estimates and human checks is a serious weakness.

Hyperparameters such as rank, layer, lambda, and prompt-pair selection appear tuned on the same benchmark categories used for final evaluation, raising overfitting concerns. The layer-injection description is also inconsistent: the main text says layers 17-18, while the appendix says the update is applied to cross-attention modules in every double block.

The technical presentation has notation and derivation issues. Eq. 6 reuses the symbol x-hat inconsistently, and the closed-form update is essentially a rank-1 projection of the refusal vector, not a true low-rank weight update. The 'low-rank refusal vector' framing is therefore misleading.

The paper does not convincingly establish permanence or irreversibility of the weight edit. There is only a limited adversarial-prompt study in the appendix and no evaluation of concept recovery through subsequent fine-tuning, prompt optimization, or model merging.

Reproducibility details are insufficient: FVD reference videos are not specified, seeds and sampling procedures are unclear, and the promised code/data are not available in the submitted manuscript. The results therefore cannot be independently verified.

strengths: Introduces the first training-free, closed-form weight update framework for concept removal in video diffusion models, which is a practically relevant contribution for safe video generation.
The low-rank refusal vector combined with contrastive PCA is a sensible adaptation of existing ideas to the video setting, and the closed-form weight absorption is technically sound.
Reports substantial censorship reductions on Open-Sora/T2VSafetyBench and ZeroScopeT2V/SafeSora while often maintaining FVD and MM-Notox close to the baseline.
Includes useful ablations on rank, suppression strength, prompt pairs, neutral set sampling, and adversarial robustness, supporting the design choices.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not fully convincing for a state-of-the-art claim: NullSCE is only compared on Open-Sora/T2VSafetyBench, SAFREE only on ZeroScopeT2V/SafeSora, and no cross-comparison is provided. This undermines the conclusion that the method consistently outperforms existing approaches.

The mathematical notation contains a dimensional inconsistency: R is defined as H x N, but the covariance C_r = \bar{R}^T \bar{R} is said to be H x H, whereas it would be N x N unless the data matrix is stored differently.

Some reported metrics do not consistently support the claims: FVD worsens for Public Figures in Table 1, and MM-Notox worsens for Sexual and Animal Abuse categories in Table 2, despite the text stating preservation or improvement.

The GPT-4o-based censorship evaluation is not fully transparent: the exact judge prompt and aggregation protocol are not provided, and reliance on a proprietary evaluator limits reproducibility and may introduce bias.

Novelty is incremental: refusal vectors, closed-form concept editing, and contrastive PCA are existing components; the main contribution is their adaptation to video diffusion rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Hyperparameter and implementation details are somewhat inconsistent: the main text selects layers 17-18, while the appendix describes updating cross-attention modules in all double blocks or up-blocks depending on the model.
